questions.q: In a point-to-point message queue, how many consumers process a given message?
options: Every subscribed consumer processes a copy
Exactly one consumer processes it
Zero consumers, by design
All consumers process it simultaneously in a race
questions.explain: A point-to-point queue delivers each message to exactly one consumer, making it well suited to distributing discrete units of work across a pool of workers.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of putting a message broker between a producer and a consumer?
options: It makes the producer and consumer share the same process
It decouples them — the producer only needs the broker to be up, not the consumer, right now
It guarantees the consumer never needs to process the message
It eliminates the need for any network at all
questions.explain: A broker lets the producer publish and move on without needing the consumer to be live and reachable at that exact moment, which is the core decoupling benefit.

questions.q: What distinguishes a log-based stream (Kafka-style) from a classic point-to-point queue?
options: A stream can only ever have one consumer
A stream keeps a durable, ordered log that multiple independent consumer groups can each read at their own pace
A stream deletes each message immediately after it's published
A stream cannot preserve message order
questions.explain: Log-based streaming retains an ordered log and offsets per consumer group, allowing independent progress and replay — something classic queues and pub/sub generally don't support.

questions.q: What risk does at-most-once delivery carry?
options: Messages are always delivered more than once
A message can be silently lost if something fails before delivery is confirmed
It requires a consensus protocol to function at all
It guarantees duplicate processing
questions.explain: At-most-once prioritizes speed over reliability: if a failure occurs before confirmation, the message may simply never arrive, with no retry to recover it.

questions.q: How do most systems that claim "exactly-once" delivery actually achieve it?
options: By using a perfectly reliable network that never drops messages
By combining at-least-once delivery with deduplication on the receiving side
By sending every message exactly one time with no retries
By disabling all message brokers
questions.explain: True exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is extremely hard to guarantee. In practice, systems retry (at-least-once) and deduplicate on receipt, which is more accurately called "effectively-once."
